title: Risks and failure modes
task_statement: Map each risk to a prevention control, a detection signal, and a recovery step. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Hallucination control with grounded quotes
components.first_principle: A claim that cites a quote from the source is checkable, and a claim without a quote is removed.
steps: Allow Claude to say that it does not know when the source lacks the answer.
For long documents, ask Claude to extract exact quotes before it answers.
Limit the answer to facts that appear in the quotes or the supplied documents.
Ask Claude to attach a source quote to each claim.
Remove each claim that has no source quote from the final text.
Check the citations in application code before the reader sees the answer. (Inference)
Review high-stakes answers with a person, because these techniques reduce errors but do not catch every error.
pros: Makes each claim checkable against a quote in the source.
Lowers the rate of false statements in long documents.
Works through prompt design, without a separate grounding service.
cons: Quote extraction adds tokens and latency to each call.
The techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them.
A quote can support a wrong claim when the source document is wrong. (Inference)
use_when: Answers must cite a source document.
The input is a long document, such as a policy or a report.
A wrong claim has a cost for the user or the business.
do_not_use_when: The task is open fiction with no source requirement.
The answer needs live data that no supplied document or tool provides.

constraints.choice: Ask for quotes first and the answer second, in one prompt.
constraints.combination: Split the work into two calls when the document is very long. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Quote only the passages that matter, not the full document.
Use best-of-N comparison only for high-stakes answers.
constraints.combination: Compare outputs for inconsistencies that point to a hallucination.

constraints.choice: Log each quote and claim pair for each answer.
constraints.combination: Alert on claims that arrive without a quote. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Write the instruction so that no quote means no claim.

components.exam_tie: D5.2. Expect a scenario where a fluent answer cites nothing. The credited answer requires grounded quotes and removes unsupported claims. (Inference)
components.trap: A larger model looks like the fix for unsupported claims. The docs describe quotes, permission to abstain, and citations for the same risk.
components.decision_rule: Require a source quote for each claim, and remove each claim that has none.
components.exam_tip: If the scenario asks for a control on unsupported claims, choose quotes and citations over a model change.

components.name: Cost exhaustion limits
components.first_principle: A spend limit on a workspace caps the monthly loss, and a call cap in code stops one runaway run.
steps: Create a workspace for each project, team, or environment that calls the API.
Set a monthly spend limit on each workspace in the Console.
Configure spend alerts at the thresholds that you choose.
Set rate limits for each model in the rate limit settings of each workspace.
Expect the organization limits to apply, even when workspace limits add up to more.
Cap the number of tool calls in each run in application code. (Inference)
pros: Caps monthly spend per workspace without a code change.
Separates usage by project, team, or environment.
Sends an alert at each threshold that you set.
cons: You cannot set a spend limit on the Default Workspace.
Spend can take about 2 hours to show recent usage, so usage can pass a limit before requests fail.
A spend limit does not stop a single run that loops in minutes. (Inference)
use_when: Several teams share one organization and need separate budgets.
A new workflow could loop or flood the API.
Finance needs a monthly ceiling for each project.
do_not_use_when: The only key runs in the Default Workspace, because you cannot set a spend limit on that workspace.
The control must stop one run within minutes. Use a call cap in code instead. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Set a monthly spend limit for each workspace.
constraints.combination: Add alerts at thresholds below the limit.

constraints.choice: Set workspace rate limits for each model, for requests and tokens.
constraints.combination: Expect the organization limit to apply even when workspace limits add up to more.

constraints.choice: Use one workspace for each team so that budgets stay separate.
Export usage by API key and model when spend rises.
constraints.combination: Retire the key that drives the increase. (Inference)

native_services.text: Rate limits are managed by Anthropic. Set organization and workspace spend limits in the Claude Console. Spend can take about 2 hours to show.
Rate limits and quotas are managed by AWS. The default quota is 2 million input tokens per minute.

components.exam_tie: D5.2. Expect a scenario with a runaway loop or a budget breach. The credited answer sets a workspace spend limit with alerts, and it caps calls in code. (Inference)
components.trap: A higher rate limit looks like a fix for a cost problem. It allows more calls, so it raises spend.
components.decision_rule: Set a monthly spend limit on each workspace, and cap the calls per run in code.
components.exam_tip: If the scenario names the Default Workspace, remember that you cannot set a spend limit on it.

components.name: Fixed model IDs and retirement
components.first_principle: A pinned model ID keeps behavior fixed, and a tested migration plan handles the retirement date.

nodes.label: Usage export by key and model

steps: Name the model ID in each request, not an alias.
A dateless model ID from the 4.6 generation maps to one fixed snapshot.
Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of a model ID.
Export usage by API key and model to find deprecated model use.
Test a replacement model well before the retirement date.
Move traffic to an active model ID before retirement, because requests to retired models fail.
pros: Keeps behavior stable for a given model ID.
Gives a notice period before retirement.
Lets you find deprecated use in the usage export.
cons: A pinned ID needs a planned move when the model retires.
Deprecated models are likely to be less reliable than active models.
A replacement model can change results, so it needs its own tests.
use_when: Output must stay stable for an audited workflow.
A release needs one fixed model for a validation period.
The team must show which model handled each request.
do_not_use_when: A prototype that accepts model changes without review.
A workflow that relies on an alias for an earlier model. Check its snapshot date first.

constraints.choice: Record the model ID in each release record.
constraints.combination: Require a replacement test before each model change.

components.exam_tie: D5.2. Expect a scenario about silent output change or a model near retirement. The credited answer pins a model ID and plans a tested migration. (Inference)
components.trap: An earlier alias is wrongly taken as a fixed version. A 4.6-generation ID is a snapshot, but an earlier alias points to the latest snapshot for its minor version.
components.decision_rule: Pin a model ID for each release, and move to a tested replacement before retirement.
components.exam_tip: If the scenario asks how to avoid silent change, choose the pinned ID and a replacement test.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{Which risk is in scope?} -->|Unsupported claims| B[Require quotes and remove unsupported claims]
  A -->|Runaway spend| C{Shared budget?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Workspace spend limit and alerts]
  C -->|No| E[Call cap in code]
  A -->|Model retirement| F[Pin model ID and test replacement]
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  H[Hallucination] --> Q[Quote per claim]
  Q --> R[Remove unsupported claims]
  C[Cost] --> W[Workspace spend limit]
  W --> A[Threshold alerts]
  C --> K[Call cap in code]
  M[Model change] --> P[Pinned model ID]
  P --> T[Tested replacement]
  T --> N[Notice before retirement]
